name: Aegyo sal fillers

lead: Aegyo sal (also called pretarsal fullness or a 'charming roll') is the small horizontal bulge just below the lower lashes that becomes visible when someone smiles. It is associated in Korean beauty culture with a youthful, warm expression, and some people ask for it to be created or enhanced.

Options discussed include hyaluronic acid filler, fat grafting and, in some clinics, small surgical procedures. Published work on this specific feature is mostly descriptive clinical reports and technique reviews.

paras: In clinics the roll is built with small amounts of filler or fat placed along the pretarsal area, and a clinical review describes anatomy-based injection techniques for the region [1]. Online, some members describe non-clinical routines such as pulling the lower lid down while squinting, moisturising or topical products, which are community reports rather than clinical techniques.

Clinical papers describe the periorbital area as delicate, and forum posters mention stories of filler migrating or looking uneven. Procedures should be done by qualified clinicians; surgical versions carry the usual operative risks. Home methods have no published support.

angle.text: Filler or fat placed under the lash line creates a visible roll that makes the eyes look softer and younger when smiling. Community members describe it as a way to soften a stern or tired eye expression.

lead: Aegyo sal, sometimes translated 'eye smile' and described clinically as pretarsal fullness or the 'charming roll', is the soft horizontal roll of tissue just above the lower lash line that becomes more visible when a person smiles. It makes the eyes look warmer, softer and younger, and a 2025 clinical review describes it as an aesthetically desirable feature in East Asian culture [1]. The word 'aegyo' itself refers in Korean to a cute, affectionate style of expression [2].

People who want a more visible roll have a range of routes. Clinicians describe hyaluronic acid filler placed in the pretarsal area, fat grafting that sometimes enhances the roll as a side effect of treating the under-eye hollow, and small surgical procedures that use tissue folding with an implant [1][3][4][5][6]. In looksmaxxing forums the feature is discussed as a way to soften the look of a smile, and members trade both clinical options and non-clinical routines such as lower-lid exercises, moisturiser and topical ingredients [7][8][9][10].

The published literature on this specific feature is made up of technique reviews, letters and single-group case series rather than randomised trials. Related work on the tear trough, periocular rejuvenation and the filler complication of malar oedema provides context for how the lower eyelid area is treated [3][5][6].

paras: Pretarsal fullness is the fullness of the lower eyelid tissue lying over the tarsal plate. A clinical review notes that when it is absent the lower eyelid can look flat, tired or older, and that when present it gives a youthful, expressive appearance that is considered desirable in East Asian culture [1]. Forum posters describe the same tissue in plain terms, with one calling it the fat under the eye that supports the area and gives a youthful look [10].

The roll is most visible during a smile because the lower eyelid muscle contracts and pushes the tissue upward. Because it is tied to expression, people describe it in terms of how a smile reads, not only how the eye looks at rest [7][10].

In Korean, aegyo denotes a style of cute, affectionate behaviour expressed through voice, facial expression and gesture; scholars have written about its gendered and social meanings [2]. Aegyo sal borrows the word to name the facial feature associated with that cute, friendly look.

The wider context is the changing ideal for the Asian eye region. A 2015 plastic surgery review traces the history from Mikamo's double-eyelid technique at the end of the nineteenth century and describes how ideals can be altered along four vectors (upper, lower, medial and lateral), noting that South Korea is the country that most often uses all four [11].

A 2025 review in the journal Life described anatomy-based hyaluronic acid filler techniques for pretarsal fullness (the charming roll) and for upper-lid hollowness. The authors emphasise precise placement in the correct tissue plane to avoid complications and achieve natural-looking results, and note that tailoring to the individual anatomy and cultural preference matters [1].
A 2026 letter in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology addressed pretarsal augmentation with a PLLA-b-PEG/hyaluronic acid filler and discussed the injection plane and safety considerations [6].

Autologous fat injection has been used for neighbouring problems and has been reported to enhance the roll. A 2022 series of 102 patients with a mean age of 25.9 years treated tear trough deformity with two-dimensional fat injections; the authors reported significant improvement over an average 13.2 months of follow-up, no major complications, and enhanced aegyo sal alongside improvement in dark circles [3].

A 2026 series of 32 patients who developed worse dark circles after lower eyelid blepharoplasty received fat grafting to the infraorbital region. Patient-rated dark circle improvement averaged 4.19 on a 5-point scale, and 68.7 percent reported improvement in the appearance of the pretarsal roll [5].

A retrospective series of 68 patients (mean age 32.6, 91.2 percent women) from 2021 to 2024 described capsulopalpebral fascia plication with silicone prosthesis implantation and reported increased pretarsal protrusion from 1.2 to 2.9 mm and high patient satisfaction, with late issues including prosthesis displacement in 2.9 percent and asymmetry in 4.4 percent [4][6]. The paper has since been retracted, with a retraction notice listed in MEDLINE in September 2026 [4][6].

On looksmax.org the feature appears in threads such as a 'mega thread' calling it an easy route to looking better and a discussion about whether to remove it [8][9]. Members describe it as the soft roll that turns a flat smile into a friendlier one [7].

A guide titled 'how I got aegyo sal without fillers' describes a daily routine of pulling the lower lids down while squinting, applying moisturiser, using a dermastamp and applying a topical ingredient; its author reports results after roughly a month [7]. Other members are sceptical: one who tried the exercise for a week said he expected little because the roll is fat, not muscle, and a reply suggested putting effort elsewhere [10]. In the guide's comments, one member mentions having heard stories of filler spreading to unintended areas [7].

Clinical papers stress that the periorbital area is delicate and that correct tissue plane placement is central to avoiding complications [1]. An expert consensus on hyaluronic acid fillers discusses malar oedema, a persistent swelling of the cheek and lower eyelid region linked to limited lymphatic drainage there; the authors suggest non-permanent fillers with low hydrophilicity, a pre-treatment history and patient education [6].

Surgical versions carry operative risks; the retracted 2026 series listed early swelling in about 71 percent and bruising in about 32 percent that resolved, plus the late events noted above [6]. A review of under-eye rejuvenation notes that evidence for newer products is heterogeneous [6]. Home routines such as exercises have not been studied.

Published studies are technique reviews, letters and case series. A 2025 review covers anatomy-based filler injection for pretarsal fullness [1]. A 2022 series of 102 young patients treated with fat injection reported improvement in tear trough deformity and enhanced aegyo sal, with 58.8 percent very satisfied [3]. A 2026 series of 32 patients after blepharoplasty reported improved pretarsal roll appearance in 68.7 percent [5]. A 2026 surgical series on pretarsal fullness has been retracted [4]. No randomised trials on aegyo sal fillers were found.

lore.intro: Aegyo sal is discussed on looksmax.org as an inexpensive-to-change facial feature that makes a smile look softer, with debate over filler, exercises and whether it should be kept [7][8][9].

timeline.event: Mikamo develops the double blepharoplasty technique, a starting point for modern Asian eyelid aesthetics.[11]
Seminars in Plastic Surgery review describes the evolution of idealised Asian periorbital appearance, with South Korea using all four vectors of change.[11]
Patients enrolled in a series of two-dimensional fat injections for tear trough deformity, later reported to enhance aegyo sal.[3]
The 102-patient tear trough fat injection series is published in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology.[3]
Review in Life describes anatomy-based filler techniques for the 'charming roll'.[1]
Fat grafting series after blepharoplasty reports pretarsal roll improvement; a pretarsal fullness surgical series is retracted in September.[5][6]
